nameStory: Fraser's marsh St. John's-wort honors John Fraser, a Scottish botanist who traveled extensively collecting plants in North America during the late 1700s and early 1800s. The 'marsh' part of its name hints at where you'll find this beauty – in the soggy, waterlogged areas that many plants can't tolerate. Like other St. John's-worts, it's named for the feast day of St. John the Baptist when these sunny yellow flowers traditionally bloom.
description: Fraser's marsh St. John's-wort is a medium-sized perennial wildflower that thrives in New England's wetlands and boggy areas. This sturdy plant grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat upright, branching habit. Its cheerful yellow flowers bloom in summer, creating bright splashes of color in otherwise marshy terrain. Unlike many of its St. John's-wort cousins that prefer drier ground, this species has adapted to life with wet feet.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5 petals that feel papery to the touch, blooming in loose clusters at the stem tips. Each flower has numerous prominent stamens that create a fuzzy, golden center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are oval to lance-shaped, feeling smooth and slightly thick between your fingers. Hold a leaf up to the light and you may spot tiny translucent dots scattered throughout.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems that can handle having their roots constantly wet or waterlogged, often growing in patches or small colonies in marshy ground.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, reddish-brown capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny dark seeds. The dried capsules often persist into fall and make a subtle rattling sound when shaken.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish-tinged stems that feel firm and slightly succulent, adapted to absorb and transport extra water from their soggy habitat.

habitat: Look for Fraser's marsh St. John's-wort in New England's wetlands, including bogs, marshes, wet meadows, and the soggy edges of ponds and streams. It particularly favors areas with acidic, peaty soils and can tolerate seasonal flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like sedges, cattails, and swamp milkweed.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the wet ground as smooth, reddish stems with fresh green leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from mid to late summer, creating the plant's most noticeable and identifiable stage when the sunny blossoms stand out against the green marsh vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leave behind small reddish-brown seed capsules, while the leaves may turn yellowish before dying back. The dried seed heads often persist and rattle in autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots, leaving little trace above ground except occasionally some persistent dried stems and seed capsules poking through snow or ice.

funFact: This plant is like a natural sponge with legs – it can actually help filter and clean pollutants from wetland water as it grows, making it a living water treatment system that also happens to be beautiful!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Virginia marsh St. John's-wort, which grows in similar wet habitats. Fraser's tends to be taller and more robust, while Virginia marsh St. John's-wort is typically shorter and more delicate. Remember: Fraser was a far-traveling plant collector, and his namesake plant is the larger, more adventurous-looking of the two marsh species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a St. John's-wort, some botanists now place this species in the genus Triadenum rather than Hypericum, though you'll still see both names used. This reflects ongoing scientific discussions about how closely related the marsh-loving species are to their dry-ground cousins.
compareHints: Unlike most other St. John's-worts in New England that prefer dry, sunny locations, Fraser's marsh St. John's-wort is the wetland specialist of the family. While common St. John's-wort has many more stamens per flower and grows in fields and roadsides, Fraser's has fewer stamens and strictly sticks to soggy ground. The habitat difference is usually the quickest way to tell them apart – if your feet are getting wet, you're probably looking at Fraser's!
